draft.title: Polarisation
card: Light is a transverse wave, so its electric field can vibrate in many planes. Polarisation means the vibrations are limited to one plane.
A polarising filter lets through only the part of the light vibrating along its transmission axis. Unpolarised light loses about half its intensity passing through a first filter.
Polarised light then meets a second filter at angle θ between the two axes. Malus's law gives the intensity through it: I = I₀cos²θ, where I₀ is the intensity reaching the second filter.
At θ = 0° all the light passes. At θ = 90° none passes. Only transverse waves can be polarised, so polarisation is evidence that light is a transverse wave.
draft.remember: A filter passes one plane of vibration. Through a second filter, I = I₀cos²θ.

a.q: What does polarisation of light show about the nature of light?
opts: Light travels at a fixed speed
a.why: Only transverse waves can be limited to one plane of vibration. A longitudinal wave vibrates along its direction of travel, so it has no planes to filter. Interference is shown by other waves too, so it does not point to polarisation.
a.clue: Which type of wave has vibrations at right angles to its travel?

b.q: Polarised light of intensity 80 W m⁻² reaches a second polarising filter. Its axis is at 60° to the light's plane of vibration. What intensity passes through?
b.why: I = I₀cos²θ = 80 × (cos 60°)² = 80 × 0.5² = 20 W m⁻². The tempting 40 W m⁻² comes from using cos 60° without squaring it.

problems.detail: The last sentence of why (a), 'Interference is shown by other waves too, so it does not point to polarisation', is confusing. It should say that interference shows light is a wave, but not that it is transverse, because longitudinal waves interfere too.

check.summary: The card and both questions are correct, and each has a single right answer (transverse wave; 20 W m⁻²). The only issue is a confusingly worded final sentence in the explanation for question a.

flags: Question a, wording: The last sentence of why (a), 'Interference is shown by other waves too, so it does not point to polarisation', is confusing. It should say that interference shows light is a wave, but not that it is transverse, because longitudinal waves interfere too.
